1. Mean position error and how often predictions help or hurt

What are the three models?

Plot nameSimple meaning
SingleThe model gives one predicted player position: one dot.
UncertaintyThe model gives one predicted position and a likely area around it. A larger area means more uncertainty.
MixtureThe model gives three possible areas. Each has its own center, spread and probability. The three probabilities add up to 100%.

Mixture example: area A has 60%, area B has 30%, and area C has 10% of the model probability. These are possible position areas, not action labels or accuracy percentages for exact points. Areas may overlap. The values here illustrate the format.

For the position-error comparison, we use the probability-weighted average of the three centers as one estimated position. We do not choose the center closest to the true player.

Orange bars: move at most 25 cm from librcsc. Start at the original librcsc position and move toward the model prediction, by no more than 25 cm. Validation-selected gates may also keep the original position. For example, if the model suggests a position 2 m to the right, this policy moves at most 0.25 m to the right. This limits the size of the correction; it does not intentionally add 25 cm of error, and the final error can still exceed 25 cm.

Right chart: full model predictions only. Green means the position error decreased. The warm-colored sections show how much extra error was introduced: up to 1 cm, >1–5 cm, >5–25 cm, >25–50 cm, or >50 cm. Gray means no change. The groups do not overlap and together cover all samples. The limits refer to the change in error, not the final total error.

Calibration uses ten separate validation games, with age-specific thresholds, before test evaluation. These are empirically calibrated ellipses from total predictive covariance. A mixture ellipse summarizes within-component and between-component uncertainty; it is not the full multimodal density, and individual component weights are not independently calibrated accuracy claims. Region size matters: a huge region can cover the truth without helping decisions.

Distribution modelMean negative log density (lower better)
Position + uncertainty-0.23
Three possible positions-1.07

NLL evaluates the actual Gaussian or mixture density at the held-out true position in meters. Uncertainty-ranking curves check whether low predicted uncertainty also identifies lower realized error. Neither metric alone proves that confidence gating improves decisions.

5.1 Does using only high-confidence predictions help?

80% must describe a specific event. The earlier 80% coverage row is a chosen region level, shared by all samples. Here confidence means the calibrated probability that the actual position is within a fixed distance of the point we would use: P(position error ≤25 cm), with a 50 cm sensitivity check. Thresholds are 50/80/90/95%. When rejected, use the original WM position.

Gaussian probabilities integrate its full 2D density inside the circle. Mixture probability gates integrate all three components around the highest-weight component center. Isotonic probability calibration uses only the ten calibration games. Component-weight gates are tested separately: an 80% component weight measures dominance, not 80% positional accuracy. The original weighted-mean and highest-weight-center readouts are both shown for those gates.

All percentages and means retain the full 28,180,368-row denominator. Rejected rows keep WM and have zero added error. “Worse” measures additional position error relative to WM; “Max final error” is total error. Numerical tolerance is 0.001 cm.

What to keep, and what to investigate next

In the original three-model comparison, the lowest raw mean error is Single position, at 57.22 cm versus 129.43 cm for stock WM. This identifies a candidate for further validation, not a ready live replacement.

  • Preserve trustworthy current observations. Investigate anonymous-update reliability separately before changing those tracks.
  • Use the already-accurate-stock and near-ball rows to judge practical risk, rather than ranking by the pooled mean alone.
  • Compare the capped policy when limiting severe regressions matters. It trades much of the possible correction for a bound on added position error.
  • If a distribution model has worse point error but useful confidence, a next experiment can estimate uncertainty around a frozen accurate point model. That was not trained here.
  • Repeat promising approaches with additional seeds and inspect failure trajectories before any live integration.

8. Method and limits

Named history within uninterrupted PlayOn; no current identified sighting; last identified position 1-30 cycles old; valid known-number WM position and same-cycle truth. Unknown proximity-matched tracks excluded. Equal weight per paired target-cycle.

  • All 200 source games and 4,400 observers are included in the dataset. Whole-game split: 160 train, ten selection, ten calibration, 20 test.
  • Same 51 observation features, uniform-number embedding, 64-unit GRU, 32-cycle history, sampled training endpoints and ten-epoch budget. Point output uses a distance loss; probabilistic outputs use NLL plus a distance term. One seed is tested.
  • Features retain old observed velocity/body with masks and ages even when stock WM declares its corresponding field invalid. This experiment predicts position only.
  • No fullstate, true actions, true distances or future observations enter features. Stops, setplays and cycle discontinuities reset history.
  • Checkpoint and mixture readout are selected before testing. Never choose the component closest to true test position.
  • Unknown proximity-matched tracks and rows without valid stock positions are excluded from paired gains. Results do not establish performance for gaps above 30 cycles or different teams/configurations.
  • Raw outputs and capped/gated outputs are offline comparisons. Integration consistency, decision timing and match benefit still require a later shadow/live experiment.

All exact aggregates, gates and split · Comparison tables · Saved diagnostic cases · Training and reproduction

9. Can more training, a larger network or more data help?

Four controlled changes were actually trained. Fresh width/depth/data variants used the same 2.048M sampled-endpoint budget as the original network. Continuation added another 2.048M endpoints. Checkpoints were chosen only on the selection games. The table uses one common 500,000-row subset of the old test games for every variant.

VariantParametersTrain-pool probe cmSelection cmSame test subset cmp95 cmWorse >0 cm %Worse >25 cm %Max extra error cm
Original64×1,10 epochs32,88257.8856.4157.30250.2732.809.831,242.99
64×1,20 epochs32,88254.5953.2754.10230.9532.429.371,323.74
128×1,10 epochs123,05852.3050.8251.56218.1232.149.351,273.53
64×2,10 epochs57,84254.8853.6254.43237.2832.529.371,311.61
64×1,40 training games32,88257.7856.5157.34251.2632.879.701,260.37

Full-cohort check of the validation-selected candidate: 128×1,10 epochs, 28,180,368 samples, mean error 51.46 cm, p95 217.77 cm, additional error >25 cm on 9.40% of samples. This model was chosen by selection error, not by test rank.

  • More updates helped: the original selection curve was still improving at epoch10; continued training reduced error further.
  • More width helped in this run: 128 units improved selection and test error at the same fresh-training endpoint budget.
  • A second layer also helped, but less than width for mean error: it changes both capacity and computation, so layer count alone is not a guarantee.
  • More source games alone did not visibly help at this fixed update budget: 40 and 160 games produced almost identical mean error. This does not show that additional data can never help; it isolates diversity with the same number of sampled endpoints.
  • No large train-pool/selection gap is visible in these probes. The probe is not the exact set of optimized endpoints. For the 40-game model it also includes other original training games, so it must not be read as its in-sample training error.

These are one-seed exploratory comparisons, not a search proving the best architecture. More games, more optimizer updates and deliberately covering difficult situations are separate interventions. For rare failure cases, choose sampling/weights using training/validation data while retaining natural sample weighting in evaluation.

Exact results, configurations and game split. Checkpoints and TensorBoard events remain under logs/exp5-s1/scaling-study.

10. Learn when to use a model or keep WM

Eight selector families were tested, including clustering and nearest neighbors. Each learns or estimates advantage over WM, rather than merely predicting absolute network accuracy. The three original networks are frozen. Fit uses 250,000 rows from ten selection games; thresholds and candidate selection use 500,000 rows from ten separate calibration games. All candidates below are compared on the same one-million-row old-test subset.

Inputs are observer features, position age/count, uniform-number category, proposed correction and observable motion/context. Two different objectives: “mean” maximizes predicted error reduction. “risk” additionally penalizes the magnitude of harmful replacements: utility = gain − 3×max(−gain,0), where gain = WM error − model error. This risk objective is a preference, not a bound or guarantee. The severity-weighted classifier wins both validation comparisons. Its score is not a calibrated probability that the model wins.

What we learned: predicting relative advantage is more useful than treating mixture dominance as correctness. The mean-focused single-position selector slightly improves the original network mean and substantially reduces how often it worsens WM. The risk-focused selector reduces harmful replacements further, at some cost in mean accuracy. The three-network selector offers another tradeoff; it does not dominate the simpler selector on all metrics. Rare large regressions remain, and fallback can retain a large WM error.

Scope of this original selector study: these selectors use the original 64-unit networks. The later refinement study in sections11–16 tests GRU128 routing, harm-aware retraining, bounded corrections and new-game confirmation. Keep these stages separate when comparing gains.

Research and targeted training

The literature supports selective prediction, learning to defer and estimating local competence. We tested gradient-boosted advantage estimators, clustering and nearest neighbors here. Verified research notes and eight ranked approaches include SelectiveNet, Learning to Defer, and DESlib. These references motivate methods; they do not certify this soccer experiment.

For targeted retraining, label harmful cases on training data, study observable groups and oversample or reweight them using validation feedback. Keep natural per-sample weighting for evaluation. A comparison using additional seeds, hard-case weighting and a fresh game set has not yet been run; we do not claim those improvements. Correlated player cycles also mean that row-level confidence or conformal terminology cannot automatically establish game-level guarantees.

Evaluation limit: the old 20 test games were previously inspected. These new comparisons are exploratory reuse, even though fit and threshold tuning use separate validation games. No live changes or match-win claims follow from these position metrics.

All selector candidates and exact results · Multi-expert results. Serialized offline estimators remain under logs/exp5-s1/selector-study.

11. Final refinement: focus on useful distances and harmful replacements

Scope: position only, observation gaps in the same unquantized-vision adaptive-view configuration. No changes are applied to live agents. Each stage below has a separate result. Distance rule: “under 50 m” means the server’s true observer–target distance at the current cycle is strictly below 50 m. This is a reporting label only. Runtime selection and distance-focused tuning use the distance estimated from the unmodified WM and observer position. The two masks are deliberately different.

12. Can a small readable decision tree choose well?

We fitted depth 2/3/4/5 trees using either expected gain or severity-weighted winner labels. Simple rules use position count, then speed, then disagreement distance. Strong comparators use 180 boosted trees. Tree inputs are 14 named observable features; boosted models add the existing observer/context and uniform-number features. Fit: 250k selection rows. Thresholds/objectives: 500k separate calibration rows. Every selector preserves WM when posCount is zero. Additional-error thresholds allow0.001cm numerical tolerance.

Short method guide: gain tree predicts how many meters the model saves. Weighted winner tree learns which estimate wins, giving larger mistakes more weight. A classifier score is not an ordinary correctness probability. A small tree is easy to inspect; the boosted selector can represent more detailed combinations.

13. Train the model to avoid harmful replacements

Controlled fine-tuning starts from the same GRU128 checkpoint and uses identical sampled endpoints. The ordinary continuation is the control. Harm penalty adds λ×max(model error−WM error,0) to ordinary position error. A fourth variant additionally gives 4× training weight to rows where WM error is below 25 cm. Truth is used only for training labels/weights; runtime inputs do not change. Fresh seeds repeat ordinary GRU128 training separately.

Additional residual candidate: reuse the GRU128 encoder, zero the new readout and learn corrections around current WM instead of around constant-velocity extrapolation. It therefore starts by preserving WM exactly. It uses the same inputs, an additional 2.048M sampled endpoints and harm penalty1. This exploratory amendment is recorded before any new-game performance is evaluated.

14. Blend or cap the correction instead of replacing it fully

Blending moves partway from WM toward the network (25/50/75/100%). Capping then limits that movement to 25/50/100/200/400 cm or leaves it uncapped. Adaptive caps instead grow by 10/25/50/100 cm per cycle since the last named sighting, up to 1/2/4 m; these are tested with 50%/100% blending. We compare unconditional use and frozen learned selector scores. All choices are tuned on calibration games; rejected rows retain WM. A cap bounds added distance error from this correction, not final total error.

17. A tiny decision tree is a credible engineering alternative

The same-input controls fit new trees using only original selection games and tune thresholds on original calibration games. We additionally score their fixed choices on the new-game batch. This is additional exploratory reuse after primary confirmation; it does not change the original frozen policies or serve as another untouched confirmatory test.

MethodSelector sizeAll mean cmUnder50m mean cmUnder50m worse >0cm %>25 cm %>50cm %Max added error m
Mean focused: boosted180 trees45.5549.3713.967.693.2612.39
Mean focused: simplified tree7 nodes45.9049.7214.437.803.3712.39
Practical: boosted180 trees48.3452.305.433.641.7011.82
Practical: simplified tree11 nodes49.6953.656.403.531.8811.82

Accuracy versus complexity: the small mean-focused tree adds only 0.35 cm to mean error below 50 m compared with 180 boosted trees. The small practical tree adds1.35 cm; its >25 cm-harm rate is slightly lower, while its any-harm rate is higher. Neither choice wins every metric.

At each fixed threshold, branches whose leaves all make the same final choice can be merged. The 15-node mean tree becomes 7 nodes; the 49-node practical tree becomes 11 nodes. This preserves the decision for every input by construction; both exports also matched their original tree on all 500,000 calibration rows. No retraining or threshold change occurs. The compact trees output a choice, not calibrated confidence; changing the decision threshold requires exporting a new compact tree.

The actual seven-node mean-focused rule

First preserve WM for posCount0 and other ineligible cases. Then use this learned rule. “Correction” is the distance between the raw network prediction and WM; age is cycles since the last confirmed named sighting. Unknown ball position uses the same fallback as the training features.

Displayed thresholds are rounded. The exact exported trees retain full-precision thresholds and the float32 input contract.

The eleven-node practical rule
if correction_norm <= 0.717385:
  if correction_per_cycle <= 0.0517116:
    KEEP WM
  else:
    if wm_ball_distance <= 1.31962:
      KEEP WM
    else:
      if correction_per_cycle <= 0.325896:
        if last_speed <= 0.112358:
          USE MODEL
        else:
          KEEP WM
      else:
        USE MODEL
else:
  USE MODEL

What we learned, and what is worth keeping

  • More optimizer updates helped. Ordinary continuation gave the strongest mean-focused neural candidate.
  • Training against harmful replacements helped a different objective. The WM-centered residual network and a severity-aware selector gave the designated practical policy.
  • Heavy weighting of already-good WM rows did not win the validation selection. Its lower regression frequency came with a larger mean-error cost.
  • Extra context and selector complexity had small returns for mean accuracy. A seven-node choice rule preserved almost all of the boosted selector’s mean improvement. Risk-focused comparisons still show tradeoffs.
  • Fixed or age-dependent partial corrections did not beat the uncapped choices on the selected validation utilities. Hard ceilings remain explicit alternatives when bounding the size of a harmful correction matters more than mean accuracy.

What remains imperfect: below 50 m, when WM already had <10cm error, its mean 1.39 cm became 4.47 cm under the primary boosted practical policy. For gaps above 10 cycles, WM mean 557.36 cm became 171.66 cm, but the largest observed added error remained 11.82 m. The largest fresh-game regressions occurred after 29-cycle gaps. Hidden actions during a long gap remain ambiguous.

For targets estimated within 2 m of the ball and truly within 50 m of the observer, the primary boosted practical policy reduced mean error from 31.35 to 24.19 cm;1.09% were made >25 cm worse. This is a position diagnostic, not a measured pass or possession benefit.

Engineering candidates retained: continued GRU128 + seven-node tree for low mean error with a simple selector; WM-centered residual GRU128 + eleven-node tree for a practical accuracy/risk tradeoff. The 180-tree versions retain the primary frozen-policy evidence and the best tested mean. Hard correction caps are separate choices with a substantial average-error cost.

Inputs, outputs, resets, coordinate handling and future integration handoff. Preserve the unmodified WM feature stream and the trained rolling 32-cycle history. A future shadow/live test must measure decision timing, state consistency and corrected-agent feedback separately.
